extracted.intended_audience: corporate executives, investor-relations/public-relations teams, and outside counsel for companies undertaking an initial public offering (IPO)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and legal guidance for what a company may and may not say (and how) during the IPO process, including safe harbors, prohibited statements, internal policies, and interactions with media, analysts, and investors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on offers (Section 5 / gun‑jumping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5 of the Securities Act prohibits making written offers to sell common stock in an IPO until a registration statement that includes a prospectus with a price range is on file, and prohibits sales until the registration statement is declared effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SEC views a wide range of communications as 'offers' or attempts to condition the market; "gun‑jumping" can lead to strict liability for unvetted statements, an SEC‑imposed "cooling off" period delaying the IPO, or rescission rights for purchasers. Companies should avoid any mention of an offering because such mentions make most safe harbors unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing to begin communication restrictions (when to be careful)
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should begin to take care regarding communications when they begin the IPO process, no later than the time the company has engaged its underwriters; executives should avoid public statements or discussions about a potential IPO even before that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any mention of an offering removes safe harbors. The practical trigger is engagement of underwriters, but caution should begin earlier; consult counsel early regarding communications practice and policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quiet period duration and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A quiet period begins when the IPO process begins and continues through consummation of the offering until 25 days after the date of offering, after which dealers are no longer required to deliver a prospectus in connection with sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During this period avoid discussions about the offering; maintain ordinary‑course communications only if consistent with past practice. The quiet period affects availability of safe harbors and delivery requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally permissible communications (ordinary‑course/factual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications that are generally permitted include normal advertising of products and services, dissemination of regularly released factual information to non‑investors, participation in trade shows and trade press articles, responses to factual inquiries unrelated to the IPO, and announcements to the media about factual business and financial developments, provided each is consistent with past practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissibility depends on consistency with historical practice and that the information is factual and unrelated to the offering or the company's prospects. Even permissible communications are often reviewed by company and underwriter counsel prior to release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally prohibited communications (conditioning the market / forward statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibited communications include new or significantly expanded corporate branding advertising campaigns; statements or forecasts about revenues, income, growth prospects or industry growth (even vague forward statements like 'We expect to continue to grow'); discussions with media or public announcements regarding the IPO, business strategy, financial performance, or prospects; discussions with securities analysts except as permitted in due diligence; participation in investor/analyst conferences except roadshow; and advertisements of the common stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid any messaging that could be seen as conditioning the market or hyping the offering. These prohibitions apply equally to digital and traditional channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital communications and social media scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: The same rules apply to digital communications as to traditional forms: websites, digital advertising, social media presence and other digital communications must be subject to the same scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies should not increase Internet presence during the IPO process; adopt internal policies limiting employee posts about the company (including on personal social media), and have counsel review digital content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designate authorized spokespersons
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should designate one or two senior officers to respond to all contacts by investors and the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting spokespeople reduces risk of inconsistent statements and helps ensure counsel review and preclearance procedures are followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit communications to factual matters and past practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should limit communications to factual matters, continue to conduct business in a customary manner, and avoid or limit dealings with the press; communications should be consistent with past practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency with historical timing, manner and form is crucial to remaining within safe harbors (e.g., Rule 169). Avoid forward‑looking statements about growth or prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record retention of communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should retain detailed records of all press releases, speeches, presentations, advertising and other communications to show there has been no increase in frequency or change in content in connection with the IPO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documented records support reliance on safe harbors and provide evidence if SEC questions whether communications conditioned the market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counsel review and preclearance of public communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Counsel should review all public communications prior to release, and counsel should preclear any media interview, conference presentation or other public speaking request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both company and underwriters' counsel typically review communications during the IPO process to ensure compliance, inclusion of required legends, and to avoid prohibited statements; clearance prevents inadvertent gun‑jumping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit employee posting of company information online
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should adopt a policy prohibiting employees from posting company information online (including personal social media, online discussions, and chat rooms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with policies, internal communications can leak; companies must be mindful that leaks may create liability or delay the IPO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure directors and senior management understand communication limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should ensure that directors and senior management understand limitations on communications during the IPO process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeted training or guidance reduces risk of off‑hand comments that could be treated as offers or conditioning the market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 169 safe harbor for regularly released factual business information
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 169 provides a non‑exclusive safe harbor for communications of factual business information (historical, not forward‑looking) if: the issuer previously released similar information in the ordinary course; timing/manner/form are materially consistent with past releases; the information is intended for non‑investors (customers/suppliers); and it is released by employees/agents who historically provided such information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communications relying on Rule 169 must not contain any information about the offering. The safe harbor is narrow and requires careful documentation of historical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 163A safe harbor (communications >30 days before public filing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 163A creates a safe harbor for communications more than 30 days before the public filing of a registration statement (note: 'filing' means public filing, not confidential submission) if: the communication does not reference the IPO; it is made by the company or an authorized representative (not an underwriter); and the company takes reasonable steps to prevent distribution or publication during the 30 days immediately before filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of interviews given more than 30 days before filing but published within 30 days; such timing traps can convert permissible communications into prohibited ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited content notices (Rules 134 and 135)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules 134 and 135 provide narrow safe harbors for issuing limited press releases or notices: Rule 135 permits notice before filing that a company proposes to make a public offering; Rule 134 permits very limited advertisements of a security after the registration statement is publicly filed. Only basic information (e.g., company name and terms of the security) may be released under these rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These safe harbors are narrow and seldom used except in special circumstances (e.g., needing to notify customers or suppliers). Use only with counsel guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow definition of oral offers
rubrics_metrics.description: The SEC's interpretation treats almost all communications as 'written' (including broadcasts, most electronic communications, and broadly disseminated voicemail); only certain real‑time, individualized telephone voicemail messages or live, real‑time presentations (including live webcasts) qualify as oral offers. On‑demand webcasts are treated as written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 'oral' is narrowly defined, companies generally avoid making any offers (oral or written) until written offers are permitted; avoid broadly disseminated 'oral' communications that may actually be treated as written.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written offering materials and Free Writing Prospectuses (FWPs)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statutory prospectus (including an estimated price range) is on file, a company may use it to make offers. Free Writing Prospectuses (FWPs) may be used only if the statutory prospectus accompanies or has preceded the FWP; FWPs generally must be filed with the SEC when used and are treated as prospectuses under federal securities laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad dissemination of FWPs is usually infeasible except via electronic forms with an active hyperlink to the statutory prospectus or to potential investors known to have received the most recent statutory prospectus. FWPs carry the same liability risk as the statutory prospectus, should be cleared with counsel, include required legends, and underwriters should be informed of intended use. FWPs are primarily used for roadshow updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity and media communications (media FWPs and paid publicity prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Company representatives should not comment on the IPO. A media story resulting from a company interview may be treated as a 'media FWP' (a type of FWP) and, if so, must be filed with the SEC unless previously filed; media FWPs are treated as prospectuses and can create liability for material misstatements or omissions. Companies may not pay for or solicit media publicity in a way that would require delivering a statutory prospectus along with such coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid granting interviews that could create media FWPs; do not pay for publicity or solicit coverage that would trigger prospectus delivery obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing the waters with qualified institutional buyers and accredited investors
rubrics_metrics.description: Since December 3, 2019, all companies may engage in written and oral communications to qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) or accredited investors at any time before or after filing a registration statement ('testing the waters').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testing the waters is common but companies should consult counsel and underwriters before engaging; expect the SEC to request copies of written materials used; each bank will have formal processes and guidelines for these activities.
